reviews.title: Price hikes, no cruelty free qualification
reviews.content: This went up in price from $8 to $10 to now $15 in about two years (2024-2026) while the catalog was still heavily expanding and lacked tons of basic brands and products. Of huge significance to some of us, Yuka still has NO cruelty-free marker or notation for animal testing. Its recommendations for “cleaner” subs are often nothing like the original search and yield literally no benefit to the discerning consumer who already knows better. Moreover, there are misrepresentations about the better-scoring cosmetic products since the statistics purport to assess safety through ingredient examination of previously tested ingredients that are toxic, banned, or whatnot without ever disclosing the exact amounts of the ingredients. This is a problem because some of the j ingredients are not bad at the percentages they are in the formulas and only pose mild threats when they aggregate on your skin, for example. This is coming from someone who’s been “natural” for almost 2 decades now. This is totally overpriced for what it is now. If you must, download it for a little bit and figure out what works for you. But don’t rely fully on their representations without doing your own diligence. It’s lowkey fear-mongering.

reviews.content:
I’ve lost confidence in Yuka’s food ratings. The scoring system oversimplifies nutrition and can be very misleading. A minimally processed food like pure butter receives a poor score largely because of its naturally occurring saturated fat, while more processed alternatives may score higher.

reviews.title: Great concept, but the database needs cleanup
reviews.content:
I use this app all the time and really appreciate having a quick way to check ingredients while shopping. It’s been a helpful tool for making healthier choices.

My biggest frustration is that the product database can be inconsistent and confusing. For example, I searched for CHOMPS beef sticks and found the exact same product listed not once, not twice, but 3x or more— some were “Bobby Approved” while the others received a thumbs down. That makes it hard to know which rating is actually correct.

I also think duplicate products should be prevented. If someone scans an item that’s not already in the database and enters the brand and product information, that should become the single listing for everyone to use rather than allowing multiple duplicate entries with conflicting ratings.

Overall, it’s a great app with a lot of potential, but cleaning up duplicate listings and ensuring products have one accurate, consistent rating would make it much more reliable.

reviews.title: Great App, Needs Some Work
reviews.content: I love this app and really appreciate being able to filter unwanted ingredients when shopping. The search query in this app really needs some work. You can search for “Shampoo” and barely have anything pop up but then if you scan something if will show it when it didn’t just by search. You can barely misspell something and it will have zero search results. Also a lot of the “related” products are super random. For example, if you scan something and it is not approved like a shampoo, the approved suggested products could be hand soap. Additionally, certain products will be non-GMO but not be approved because it has natural flavors or scents. A lot of the time this means it is a trade secret. Love the app but it needs a few tweaks to be more user friendly. I end up having to use Yuka to cross reference products because I cannot find them on Bobby Approved or cannot find good related products.

reviews.title: SHOULD BE BANNED FROM THE APPSTORE FOR VIOLATING SAFETY
reviews.content:
I’ve seen multiple products where the scoring is clearly incorrect. For example, some chip brands like Cheetos I’ve seen receive scores as high as 93 despite being loaded with additives. This app shouldn’t score additives in a way that makes them seem like minor concerns, and especially not give high ratings to items like Flamin Hot Cheetos Poffs.

When I questioned the AI about these scoring errors, it told me that it would flag the item for review. However, when I asked for more information about the flagging process, the AI contradicted itself and admitted that it doesn’t actually have access to flag or report items.

I understand that AI can make mistakes, but it shouldn’t claim that it performed an action when it has no ability to do so. Between the inaccurate scores and the AI giving me misleading information about reporting errors, I don’t feel like I can trust the app’s ratings.

reviews.title: Predatory gross business practices - avoid
reviews.content:
Update: the developer response did nothing to address these concerns. They just shift the accountability to Apple to manage their subscriptions and act as if they couldn’t possibly do something else to better support customers. 

Why not give reminders about how much time is left to cancel right in the app? Make it easier? Because you want people to forget and have to pay you! That’s predatory and ableist, no way around it. 

Read the fine print!! The seven day free trial is actually only six days. You have to cancel 24 hours before it ends to avoid being charged. 

Not only that, but despite having lower cost monthly subscriptions available they charge you for a FULL YEAR if you don’t cancel in time. 

There’s no need for this, they could just have the free features stop working after seven days instead of charging people. The least they could do is be up front and clear about exactly when and how to cancel and encourage you to screen shot it before agreeing to the trial. 

Even after paying a high fee, they still embed GLP-1 ads for you to open throughout the app disguised as opportunities to “learn more” about a food ingredient. 

This app could be great if the company genuinely cared about honesty/ethics as much as $$$. I won’t be subscribing again. Not that they care, because they have built their business on scamming new people into paying instead.

reviews.title: Good app just minor accuracy issues
reviews.content:
I’ve been using this app for over a year now (paid version), so clearly I see the value in it. I genuinely like the concept and what it’s trying to do. It’s super helpful for making better choices and being more aware of what you’re putting in your body. That’s the reason I’ve stuck with it this long.

That said, there are a few things that need serious improvement.

First, accuracy. Some of the product ratings don’t seem reliable. I’ve come across items where the information feels off, and it makes it hard to fully trust the app. There needs to be better verification, whether that’s through a stronger AI system or more consistent database checks.

Second, the search feature is frustrating. I’ll type in a product and it doesn’t show up, but then I scan it and suddenly it’s there. That makes no sense. If the item exists in the system, it should show up when searched. This becomes a bigger issue when you don’t have access to the barcode and are relying on typing it in.

Lastly, inconsistency between similar products. I scanned the same brand and product (lemon juice), just different sizes, and got completely different ratings. The ingredients matched, so there’s no clear reason for the difference. That’s confusing and makes it hard to trust the scoring system.

Overall, I like the app and still use it, but if accuracy and consistency were improved, it would be way more reliable and worth the price.

reviews.author: Sierra M. Reviews

reviews.title: Extensive onboarding, forced to free trial
reviews.content:
The onboarding experience creates unnecessary friction for a product that’s supposed to offer a free trial. Even though billing runs through Apple subscriptions (so you’re not directly entering payment details), users still have to subscribe upfront before they’ve had a real chance to explore the product.

The predictable outcome is that many people — myself included — immediately cancel the subscription after signing up so they don’t risk being charged later. Once a user has already canceled, the likelihood of them returning to renew is much lower, which ultimately works against long-term adoption.

A better customer experience would allow users to try a limited version of the product first, demonstrate value quickly, and then ask for a subscription after they’ve decided it’s worth keeping. Strong products retain customers through value, not by creating cancellation risk or onboarding fatigue.

I wanted to like this product, but I already have a negative experience associated with it before I’ve even used the product.

reviews.title: MUST HAVE IN A TOXIC WORLD!
reviews.content:
I’ve been using the Olive app to scan food products, and it’s honestly eye-opening. You just scan a barcode and it quickly breaks down ingredients, showing what’s potentially toxic or problematic and what’s actually clean. It’s helped me realize how many “healthy-looking” foods still contain additives, seed oils, or questionable ingredients.

I love that it takes the guesswork out of grocery shopping and makes ingredient labels easy to understand—especially when shopping for kids or trying to support gut health. I’ve already swapped several pantry staples for better alternatives because of this app.

If you care about what’s in your food and don’t want to stand in the aisle Googling every ingredient, Olive is 100% worth it.

reviews.title: Contradicting App
reviews.content:
I really wanted to love the Olive app, but after using it less than 30 minutes, I knew it wasn’t for me. I signed up for the 3-day trial, canceled the same day, and still got charged for a full year. When I checked my settings, it showed my cancellation as ending a year from now rather than immediately — which was extremely frustrating.

As for the actual functionality, the app requires you to do most of the work it advertises. You’re expected to take pictures of products, ingredients, and labels and upload them yourself to build their database — even for well-known, widely sold brands. That alone made me question the reliability and thoroughness of their system.

I also noticed inconsistencies and what seems like bias in their scoring. For example, I know MaryRuth’s Organics Multivitamins should not be showing as 0/100, especially when random foods like tortilla strips are rated 46/100. Some products even show completely different scores depending on how you search them. That makes the ratings feel arbitrary and not based on solid standards.

If you’re hoping the app tests or provides information about things like heavy metals, it does not. I haven’t seen a single product with heavy metal testing data attached, which was one of the reasons I wanted to try it.

Another inconvenience: when they suggest healthier alternatives, there are no links to purchase the items. You have to leave the app, Google every product yourself, and hunt down where to buy it. As a busy mom of four, that completely defeats the purpose of having a “convenience” app.

I should have read the reviews first, and that’s on me — but hopefully this helps someone else. At this time, I cannot recommend the Olive app.

reviews.title: BEWARE
reviews.content:
This app failed at the one thing it's supposed to do. It repeatedly marked products as safe even though they contained my listed allergen. I wasted money  on products I couldn't use. Thankfully, I have enough common sense to read the ingredient label myself before consuming anything. If I had trusted this app, the outcome could have been much worse.
Paying for a service that can't reliably perform its core function is absurd. From what it looks like, the information relies heavily on user submissions with little meaningful verification. That's not good enough when people's health is involved.
At this point, taking a picture of an ingredient label and asking AI tools to analyze it is more reliable than paying for this app. That's embarrassing.
The app feels less like a legitimate safety tool and more like a passive income stream for “wannabe influencers” who wanted to monetize an idea without putting in the work to make it dependable.
If the developers don't start taking accuracy seriously, then what is the app even useful for ? An app that gives users false reassurance (on several occasions) about allergens isn't just a bad product—it has the potential to lead to serious legal consequences if someone is harmed. Do better.

reviews.title: A game changer!!
reviews.content:
This app has turned a very overwhelming diagnosis for our daughter into a huge weight lifted off. I was given a list of foods she is allowed to eat with her intolerances and didn’t know where to begin with finding foods that fit the bill. I was very overwhelmed. 

With a fructose intolerance and a potential wheat intolerance, there was a ton of food that didn’t fit the bill and for a picky eater and a growing kid, it was scary as a mother to be faced with this, and also concern that she still gets the nutrients she needs. This app has taken away so much of the fear and overwhelm from finding a suitable diet for her that won’t cause her pain. 

That being said, It is always good to double check the ingredients against your recommended diet list and what is in the store because in some instances there can be inconsistencies, just due to the fact that each doctor’s recommendation for a particular diet may vary a bit, but I haven’t noticed many of these. 

For the weight it has taken off of me, it is so worth it!! It can pin down the foods that are okay, then I just double check it. 9 times out of 10 it’s accurate with what she needs. I highly recommend!

reviews.content: Rice, eggs, and oats. I couldn’t even tolerate protein shakes. After months of tests and doctors, I landed on a low-histamine diet. The scan feature brings up the exact list of color-coded ingredients for what I’m holding with a simple explanation as to why that ingredient may be a problem. No more standing forever Googling and reading blogs. By having a moderate interaction designation, I have the confidence to try more foods. Searching a food also brings up multiple brands so I can see at a glance by the use of color-coded check marks whether or not it’s even worth exploring that next brand’s offerings. The bonus for me is having searchable spices. Safe foods only work when you don’t flavor them with overlooked counterintuitive ingredients. I’ve never reviewed an app before and can’t recommend this one enough.

reviews.title: steals from you & Dangerously inaccurate
reviews.content:
when i knew i couldn’t afford to pay $50+ after a week of free trial i was immediately offered a discount to $35 for the first year. signing up you even think wow this app claims they will tell you before you’re at risk of paying with notifications. NO WHERE do they say if we offer you a discounted first year price because you mark you can’t afford the full year free we take away your free trial. will be filing a consumer complaint with my state attorney general office on the fraud in intentionally taking advantage of people who are low income. 

second, this app is absolutely useless. 

the app cannot handle common medical dietary restrictions- such as low oxalate for certain common kidney stones. or to consider suitability for things like diabetes. 

of the very limited options they do have built in, such as low histamine, a diet i previously had to follow-it’s absurd how most of the “safe” products they list are just random chemicals or compounds in processed foods that you’ve never heard of, not an actual food item you could eat on its own.

in my local grocery store they claim people can only eat a hand full of things from the entire full grocery store which is not accurate.  and those items are inaccurately categorized. for example it suggested the only bakery or dessert item i could eat was wild salmon fillets???

i have life threatening food allergies, which i common with people who need a low histamine diet. insanely they don’t let you just list the things you’re allergic to so it can avoid those. even common ingredients, like jalapeño, almond, mint, pineapple, or sage you can’t select.

for the few options it does let you select it does not do so accurately. for example you can indicate you can’t eat onion and be told it’s safe to eat chives by themselves.

or you can say you can’t eat capsicum and then get told to eat a variety
of raw bell pepper.

also, they don’t have the largest grocery chain in my state. and when i was scanning items at home from national stores like whole foods or trader joe’s or target or walmart it didn’t have many many common items.

the concept here is good a good future goal but right now the advertising, app store description, and free/trial/subscription all intentionally midlead you and are also predatory toward low income people specifically. 

i used the app for less than an hour of my week free trial and went to cancel and delete and found out i got charged for a year as someone who runs out of money for food every month. 

if you do not make this right by refunding the charge, i will be filing a claim through my attorney general’s office.

reviews.title: Absolutely Incredible
reviews.content: I’m not the kind of person to leave reviews, but I just can’t not recognize the amazing people at Fig. I’m writing this as someone from southern California after receiving an email about the support they’re providing for those struggling following the numerous fires we’ve been having. These people are genuinely so good. They’re seriously out here doing such amazing work, and they care so much about the people their app is helping. They are also constantly improving upon what is already a fantastic foundation, and every update makes the app even better and makes life so much easier. The communication and support has also been out of this world. I’ve had a lot of questions that I’ve gotten such better answers to from the folks at Fig than some of my doctors. I’ve also recommended this app to a friend of mine who has food sensitivities after they mentioned using a whole spreadsheet to track what foods they can or can’t have. I’m so happy to feel like I have more control over what I eat because all that information is in one place that’s so easy to use and navigate. Navigating low FODMAP elimination/reintroduction (especially while living on a college campus where I can’t always choose what ingredients are in my food) has felt incredibly daunting, tedious, and depressing at times, but Fig has truly been a light in the dark making things so much easier. I would absolutely love a feature to help me track FODMAP intake to make sure I’m not having too much of one trigger, but I’m so happy that this app just exists at all. Thank you so much for all you do and for how much you truly care.

reviews.title: Misleading and only suitable for food allergies not intolerances
reviews.content:
First off the app costs $60 which is pretty steep for something that’s so poorly designed.  It’s pretty much useless if you’re navigating food intolerances and not food allergies.  My Dr has me doing an elimination diet which involves avoiding legumes (including soybeans) and some other things.  I have no food allergies and have not marked anything as an allergy.   However ingredients listed in allergen statements still flag products as being unsafe for me.  Even if the allergen statement is specifically saying that a product was processed in a facility free of soy and other common allergens.  This causes hundreds of products to be incorrectly marked as unsafe and prevents me from being able to filter out red light items.  

So I paid $60 to still have to check the ingredients on every product my stores sell without being able to reliably filter anything out.  I have tried working with their support.  They did fix at least a couple products that were flagging for stating that they produced in an allergen free facility, so that’s something.  However their solution for the other allergen flags was for me to manually change soy to flag as green or yellow light.  Except that would cause it to flag incorrectly safe when it’s actually an ingredient.  Their next suggestion was for me to set it up exactly how it’s already set and doesn’t work.  They said they’re changing the system The so uses to be less confusing, so they know their app is functioning poorly.  But they still see fit to mislead people into paying to use it.

reviews.title: Stupid
reviews.content: If you are blind or can't read I might understand this app. But if you are fully abled why use this app? What this app does is it scans a barcode on a product that is 2 inches away from the ingredients list and then guess what the app does, it tells you the ingredients. You have to know what you're allergic to in order to use this app. Therefore you should be able to read the ingredients on the package and figure it out yourself. I just saw another review that said "I looked up this type of food and it gave me so many options of things I could have!" Google is free people. This app, to get all of its features, is not. And, again, reading the ingredients on things that are already in your hands is also free. This app also doesn't really understand that you can be allergic to one thing and not another. I downloaded it (and then never used it because I could just read the ingredients myself) because I have food allergies and I checked off "all nuts" as an absolutely not food but since the FDA says that coconut is a tree nut (it's not) the app automatically checked it as a no. I'm not allergic to coconut. I had to go back through and check off everything involving coconut. Coconut milk, coconut shavings, coconut extract, coconut fiber, etc. And I tried searching for Salmon and it wasn't even on the list. I'm also deathly allergic to the casein protein in dairy. That means any type of dairy is a no go for me. But for some reason the app didn't check off lactose or milk solids. This is a stupid app. Read the ingredients people don't waste your time (or money) on this app.

reviews.title: INACCURATE FOR SIBO/IBS
reviews.content: When I got diagnosed and realized I had to stick to a low fodmap diet, I tried every app around and spoonful on the browser was helping and accurate 99% of the time. The app had been great for a while until recently many foods suggested as safe suddenly became triggers. Furthermore, some of these were foods and brands that I seem to recall looking up in the past and weren’t safe but now suddenly were ok? I asked other fodmappers on reddit if they had noticed any change with the app accuracy with SIBO/IBS and surprisingly several had the same experience. One person who had done more research said that she found certain brands were sponsoring the company behind the app to add their app to promote their foods to people with low fodmap so people would stop avoiding them. This seems to be congruent with my experience of suddenly getting pains and bloating again after originally loving using spoonful on the web. What is even more sketchy is the thread has been ‘removed’ (likely from request from spoonful) despite not having broken any rules. I’d encourage anyone who had downloaded this app to reconsider using it in the future and just stick with the web version from now on. You are worth more than to have to deal with the flare ups and this app clearly has sold out.

reviews.title: Frustrated user…lack of kind/understanding support from Spoonful
reviews.content:
I have been locked out of my account for 3 months.  I have attempted logging in 20+ times now and one of two things happen:  I never receive an email with the login link or it takes so long for the email to come that the link expires.  When I tried contacting the developer I never saw any responses.  Then after sending a frustrated email, I finally saw a response from the CMO who was not very kind in his response (apparently his messages went to my junk mail and since they were from his email my attempts to search for spoonful did not pull his messages up).  I explained my position and the CMO has continued to interact with me in an unhelpful, unforgiving way.  I sent another response asking for someone else on the team to help me and today I received a message from the CMO stating, “It would be best to part ways.  There are lots of great apps out there”.  He sent me a link to request a refund, but apple requires a refund request be made within 2 months of purchase, which would have been March when I wasn’t having problems.  

Finally, after calling apple rather than going through the automated online refund request and talking with a supervisor I’m going to get a prorated refund for the remainder of the year, so maybe 3 more months of service refunded.  I would have rather had some help logging in and getting my full year of service but I’ll take what I can get at this point.

I do not recommend this app.

For those to be low FODMAP they have to be gluten-free. Each ingredient in the pretzel also needs to be low FODMAP. (The Monash app gives more detail regarding Low Fodmap ingredients.) After putting in pretzels, the Spoonful app gives many items a green checkmark. at a glance, I was hesitant that these items could all actually be low FODMAP. When I clicked on the ingredients, they were not listed. Many items that got the green check mark were like gift baskets that had pretzels in them. For these gift baskets of pretzels and meats and cheeses to be low, FODMAP, the meats would have to be onion and garlic free. No ingredients were listed for any of the items. I googled one of the pretzel brands to see what the ingredients are. First Ingredient is wheat. Not low FODMAP yet spoonful was giving it a green checkmark. A notation that is supposed to indicate that you can sagely eating that food. Spoonful cannot be trusted.

reviews.content:
Spoonful is immensely helpful when I’m in the grocery store and needing to quickly know what FODMAPs are present in processed foods. There’s even info from licensed nutritionists for a lot of items. If you find a product is missing, you can suggest it and they’ll add it to the database. 

This won’t tell you what particular foods like apples or Swiss cheese have; the Monash FODMAP app does that. But Spoonful will tell you what is present in say Mott’s applesauce. Spoonful  and Monash apps go together very well. 

The one thing that would put Spoonful over the top is to add restaurant menus so I can know what is safe to order. I’d also appreciate a filter for lactose-free. There is a milk-free filter, but lactose is a much more helpful category for me.

I’m 72 yrs old and recently developed allergies to most of the foods I loved. I had no idea how to find  foods that were compliant with my new . I thank God I found the SPOONFUL APP. It has everything I need. I purchased the full app which was very reasonably price . There is a free app also which is limited but it allows you become accustomed to using the app. 
The app makes meal planning a breeze. The app is very easy to use.  It has a UPC scanner . When I scan the UPC code on the item it immediately gives me a report. The report list whether a food item is compliant or not according  to the allergens that I listed in my profile. 
Also,I was at home and don’t t have an item to scan, I can type the item name in the search bar and get the same results as scanning the item. 

If you are looking for an app yo help you make good decisions at the grocery store, you just found it. 
I LOVE THIS APP and I’m sure you will, also!!

And if an item that I’m scanning doesn’t come up in the Spoonful database, you can easily submit it for them to analyze it and add it to their database, and they are really fast about doing this! Their support team is great—very responsive and helpful. My one gripe with this app is that for many items which have ingredients that are either low or high FODMAP depending on the serving size, the reviewing nutritionist often refers you to the Monash app for details on portion sizes. I wish they would just give the details right there rather than send me to another app. Thanks, Spoonful, you’re doing great work!

reviews.title: Used to love it.
reviews.content: I’ve found this app really helpful for managing my ibs symptoms by easily being able to navigate which foods could trigger a stomach spasm. Although I can’t say I’m a fan of the premium, although I do believe it’s important to support the developers. It is mainly how it was done, the free plan is not really worth it. They don’t give you many searches/scans a month. I could use up those searches/scans in one store visit. There are free apps that do the same thing. I would of preferred the option of them adding ads and giving us the option to pay a one time fee to remove them (or at least abit more affordable monthly price). At the least give a reasonable amount of searches/scans a month for free. I just feel like it’s really pushing us to pay in order to get the help we need. I suffer from a lot of illnesses, so I guess I’m just a little tired of all the extra costs there are for someone like me to just exist and feel a little less miserable. Don’t get me wrong, I’ve found the Spoonful app helpful but at this point I’ll just use a free app. Although I’m open to coming back and changing my mind if things become more balanced with how the premium is setup. Although to note even though it isn’t the developers fault, if you buy premium on an Android device and switch to Apple you will have to rebuy it. So I would just be aware if you buy the annual premium plan at a discounted cost that if you switch phone brands, you will have to repurchase the plan. The premium is NOT account based, it’s based on your Apple ID/Play Store ID.
